impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims directed to using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents covering anti-CGRP antibody treatments, after a jury had found willful infringement by Eli Lilly and no invalidity. The case involves blockbuster migraine drugs Ajovy (Teva) and Emgality (Lilly), and the reversal reinstates the jury's infringement verdict for further proceedings on remand.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for biologic drug innovators by affirming that genus claims to antibodies can satisfy written description and enablement where the specification discloses methods for making and humanizing antibodies known in the art, even with limited specific embodiments disclosed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Creates potential liability exposure for biosimilar and competing biologic drug developers who may face broader patent infringement claims based on genus-level antibody patent claims.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions by comparing emulated function calls to a model are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether damages based on foreign sales were properly awarded.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia University against Norton (Gen Digital), holding that the asserted cybersecurity patent claims are abstract at Alice step one and requiring further proceedings on step two. The court also ruled that the district court erred in allowing damages based on Norton's foreign sales and vacated the enhanced damages and attorneys' fees awards tied to an improper contempt finding.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides technology companies with stronger defenses against broad software patent claims under § 101, and limits patent damages exposure for products sold outside the United States.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting software-related patents face heightened risk of invalidity under Alice, and universities and research institutions may find it harder to enforce cybersecurity and software method patents.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights but retains the right to sue for infringement and retains other exclusionary rights has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who retain the right to sue third parties for infringement—a right not rendered illusory by the license—retain sufficient exclusionary rights to satisfy Article III standing. The court clarified that retention of meaningful exclusionary rights, even after granting an exclusive license, preserves standing to enforce patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners who license commercialization rights can structure agreements to retain litigation standing, providing flexibility in patent monetization and enforcement strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face broader exposure as patent holders with carefully structured license agreements can maintain standing to sue even after granting exclusive licenses.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether the same ideas could constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship correction.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's trade secret misappropriation verdict and vacated the reasonable royalty, exemplary damages, and permanent injunction, holding that the plaintiff failed to prove the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying ideas were generally known. The court also reversed the patent invalidity finding based on inventorship correction, since the same generally known ideas could not constitute an inventive contribution. The counterfeiting verdict was affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces that trade secret claimants must rigorously prove their information is not generally known in the industry, providing defendants with a strong defense when alleged secrets reflect commonly understood concepts.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection for product designs and methods face greater scrutiny at trial, as courts will demand specific evidence that the claimed information derives independent economic value from not being generally known.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality grounds and in striking a damages expert's theories for inadequate disclosure in damages contentions.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the district court's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent against Intel on extraterritoriality grounds, finding genuine disputes of material fact. The court affirmed the rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory and the striking of certain damages expert theories for failure to adequately disclose them. The case was remanded for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement of semiconductor and processor patents may pursue claims where at least some infringing activity occurs domestically, even if significant design and manufacturing occurs abroad.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global design and manufacturing operations remain exposed to infringement claims for products with domestic sales, and must carefully monitor opponents' damages contentions disclosures to preserve evidentiary challenges.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims relating to non-uniform constellation designs used in broadcasting, finding that some claims were directed to abstract mathematical optimization, while affirming eligibility for claims tied to specific hardware implementations. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages, preserving the jury's findings on those issues.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent claims tied to concrete hardware implementations of communication standards remain eligible, giving standards-essential patent holders a path to enforce specific apparatus claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent claims framed as mathematical optimizations in digital communications face heightened § 101 eligibility challenges, increasing invalidity risk for holders of standards-related patents with broadly drafted method claims.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether genuine disputes of material fact preclude summary judgment on inequitable conduct in patent prosecution and on a Walker Process antitrust fraud claim based on attempted monopolization.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment for both parties, finding genuine disputes of material fact on whether Tenaris committed inequitable conduct in obtaining coiled tubing patents by failing to disclose prior art CYMAX documents it had acquired, and on whether Global Tubing could establish Walker Process fraud for attempted monopolization. The case was remanded for trial on both issues.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of inequitable conduct in patent prosecution can challenge summary determinations where the evidence of intent to deceive is genuinely disputed, preserving their patent rights for trial.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who acquire prior art through corporate acquisitions face significant litigation risk if they fail to disclose that art during prosecution, potentially exposing them to both unenforceability and antitrust liability under Walker Process.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge at summary judgment, and whether pre-critical-date commercial sales of a device anticipate patent claims under the on-sale bar of 35 U.S.C. § 102(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify outside personal knowledge for summary judgment purposes, and that sales of a prior art device more than one year before the patent's priority date invalidated the claims regardless of whether the sales expressly disclosed the device's functionality.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases can rely on 30(b)(6) corporate testimony even from witnesses who joined the company after the relevant events, broadening the evidentiary tools available to establish prior art sales.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face expanded on-sale bar exposure, as commercial sales of embodying products need not publicly disclose their internal functionality to constitute invalidating prior art.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in a pharmaceutical composition patent refers to a pH measured at the standard temperature in the field, and whether the doctrine of equivalents could apply.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no literal infringement and no infringement under the doctrine of equivalents of Actelion's epoprostenol pharmaceutical patents by Mylan's proposed generic drug. The court agreed that pH claims must be interpreted according to the temperature standard recognized in the relevant scientific field, and that Actelion was barred from asserting equivalents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers gain clarity that pharmaceutical patent claims specifying pH values will be construed according to field-standard measurement conditions, facilitating design-around strategies for ANDA filers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies with composition patents must draft claims with precise measurement conditions to capture variations, as courts will apply field-standard interpretations that may narrow claim scope.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement functionality infringed Masimo's patents covering wearable physiological measurement devices, and whether Masimo established a domestic industry.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watches that infringed Masimo's patents on wearable blood oxygen measurement technology, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing models. The court found no error in the Commission's validity rulings, infringement findings, or domestic industry determination.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with domestic industry investments can effectively use ITC Section 337 proceedings to obtain exclusion orders against major technology companies importing infringing products, providing a powerful enforcement mechanism.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major consumer electronics companies face significant supply chain disruption risk from ITC exclusion orders when incorporating patented health-monitoring technologies into widely sold devices.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a patent plaintiff's damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report in a patent infringement case against Microsoft's Azure platform, finding the district court applied an improperly rigid standard. The court vacated the summary judgment granted to Microsoft based on absence of a remedy and the denial of Exafer's motion to reopen discovery, remanding for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent plaintiffs gain greater flexibility in presenting damages evidence, as appellate courts will scrutinize district court exclusions of expert testimony for overly rigid application of Daubert standards in patent cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending patent suits face prolonged litigation exposure when damages expert exclusions are reversed, increasing settlement pressure and litigation costs.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action when it missed the deadline for seeking a stay of the original action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent may not circumvent the statutory deadline for obtaining a mandatory stay of a parallel district court action by dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action. The court ruled that allowing such a tactic would undermine the time limits Congress imposed in § 1659(a) and permit gamesmanship to delay resolution of patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the assurance that ITC respondents cannot manipulate procedural deadlines to indefinitely delay parallel district court patent litigation through strategic refiling of declaratory judgment actions.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay lose the ability to pause parallel district court proceedings, potentially forcing them to litigate on two fronts simultaneously.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, including the award of attorneys' fees, costs, and incentive awards to class representatives.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's approval of a $125 million settlement in a nationwide class action alleging the federal judiciary charged excessive PACER fees to fund expenses unrelated to operating the PACER system. The court upheld attorneys' fees, costs, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, rejecting an objector's challenges to jurisdiction, settlement fairness, and the propriety of incentive awards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Validates the use of class actions to challenge excessive government fees and supports the availability of incentive awards for nonprofit class representatives who serve the interests of a broad class.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board erred in its obviousness determination of patent claims relating to sensor-based logistics systems, particularly regarding time-delayed reporting of sensor information.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's finding that challenged claims of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent were unpatentable as obvious and remanded for further proceedings. The case raised questions about potential abuse of the IPR process by Qualcomm, which filed IPR petitions challenging patents asserted against a different entity (Roambee) on the filing deadline, despite not being a party to the underlying litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners gain stronger protection against potentially coordinated or proxy IPR challenges filed by third parties near statutory deadlines, preserving the integrity of the time-bar provisions of 35 U.S.C. § 315(b).
impacts.negativeImplications: Entities seeking to challenge patents through IPR must ensure their petitions are independently motivated, as courts may scrutinize the timing and circumstances of third-party filings that coincide with related litigation deadlines.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents are invalid for omission of a coinventor when the patent holder cannot locate the omitted inventor to correct inventorship under 35 U.S.C. § 256, and whether the court may correct inventorship under § 256(b) when the missing inventor cannot be found.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that patents naming incorrect inventors are invalid where the patent holder acknowledges a coinventor's contribution but cannot locate that person to correct inventorship through § 256(a). The court also affirmed the denial of judicial correction under § 256(b), holding that the patent holder failed to meet the statutory requirements for court-ordered correction.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers gain a powerful invalidity defense when patent holders collaborate with foreign manufacturers or designers who may later become unreachable, incentivizing patent applicants to properly name all inventors from the outset.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop inventions collaboratively with foreign partners or contractors risk patent invalidation if they cannot locate all coinventors when challenged, even where the omission was not deceptive.
